# From benchmark to decision {#application}

*What happens when the data are real?*

## The transfer problem, stated honestly

A Miura sheet is not a gene expression matrix. It has intrinsic dimension two,
exact isometry to a flat chart, uniform sampling density, no measurement model,
no zero inflation, no batch effect and no discrete cell identities. Nothing
about a folded piece of paper says anything about haematopoiesis. If the
argument of this book were "crease patterns resemble transcriptomes", the
argument would be worthless.

The argument is different. What transfers is not the data but the *failure
mode*. Three failures were measured exactly in Part III because the answer key
was available, and all three are properties of the algorithm and its input
graph, not of the biology behind that graph.

**Short circuits.** A $k$-nearest-neighbour graph built on a folded surface
acquires edges between facets that are close in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and far apart on
the sheet. One such edge collapses a geodesic and, through it, the whole
embedding — the topological instability of graph-geodesic methods
[@balasubramanian2002isomap; @tenenbaum2000isomap]. Nothing in that mechanism
refers to origami. It requires only that the ambient metric occasionally
under-estimates the intrinsic one, which is the defining situation of any
manifold with a fold in it, biological or otherwise.

**Seed variance.** t-SNE and UMAP optimise non-convex objectives from random
initialisations [@vandermaaten2008tsne; @mcinnes2018umap]. Chapter
\@ref(results) showed that within-method seed spread frequently exceeds the
between-method gap. That is a property of the optimiser and the initialisation
[@kobak2021initialization], not of the input distribution.

**Metrics that certify wrong embeddings.** Chapter \@ref(evaluation) is the
transferable result. Trustworthiness, continuity and $k$NN preservation are all
computed from the same neighbourhood structure the embedding was fitted to, so
they score an embedding on the criterion it optimised. Measured against exact
truth they were high on embeddings whose `reconstruction_error()` was large. A
metric that fails on a sheet of paper will not succeed on a count matrix; the
count matrix is strictly harder.

So the licence to transfer is narrow and specific. The benchmark tells you which
diagnostics and which metrics are trustworthy. It does not tell you what a UMAP
of your data means.

## Placing a real dataset on the $\theta$ axis

To use the Chapter \@ref(results) grid you must know which slice of it applies.
The fold angle $\theta \in [0, \pi/2)$ is a difficulty parameter with an
operational signature: as $\theta$ grows, facets approach one another in
$\mathbb{R}^3$ while staying fixed distances apart on the sheet, so the ambient
$k$NN graph acquires short-circuit edges and the local intrinsic dimension
estimated across a crease rises above two.

`foldbenchR` already localises the first of these exactly:

```{r decision-sc-theta}
library(foldbenchR)

pat <- miura_ori(n_rows = 6, n_cols = 6)

# The real graph's sample size and neighbourhood size, fixed by the
# preprocessing in the worked example below. Everything on the benchmark side
# is run at these values, not at benchmark-convenient ones: both statistics
# move with sampling density.
N_CELLS <- 2638L
K_GRAPH <- 20L

# Smallest fold angle on the grid at which the kNN graph first joins two
# facets that are far apart in the flat truth. NA if it never does.
theta_c <- short_circuit_theta(pat, k = K_GRAPH, n = N_CELLS,
                               grid = seq(0, pi / 2 - 0.05, length.out = 25),
                               seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1])
```

This is the honest pivot of the chapter, so state the limitation before using
the result. `short_circuit_theta()` needs `pattern$truth` — it declares an edge
a short circuit by looking up the true separation of its endpoints in the exact
unfolding. On real data there is no unfolding, so the function cannot be called
at all. It is a benchmark instrument, not a diagnostic.

Transferring it therefore requires an explicit argument, and the argument is
this: build a *truth-free* surrogate, then show on the benchmark that the
surrogate turns on at the angle the truth-based function reports. If the two
agree where truth is available, the surrogate is licensed where it is not. That
is a claim that can be checked rather than assumed, and the calibration figure
below is the check.

The surrogate is the detour test. Delete an edge and ask how far you must walk
to get back to where it went. A genuine local edge has a short detour through
its own neighbourhood; a short circuit has a detour the length of the fold.

```{r decision-shortcircuit}
# Short-circuit diagnostic for an arbitrary n x p data matrix.
# No ground truth required: it is a statement about the kNN graph alone.
# foldbenchR does not import these; load them explicitly.
short_circuit_index <- function(X, k = 15, n_candidates = 500, detour = 4) {
  stopifnot(is.matrix(X), k >= 2)
  n  <- nrow(X)
  nn <- FNN::get.knn(X, k = k)

  # Local scale: distance to the k-th neighbour. A per-point density estimate.
  local_scale <- nn$nn.dist[, k]

  g <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
    data.frame(
      from   = rep(seq_len(n), each = k),
      to     = as.vector(t(nn$nn.index)),
      weight = as.vector(t(nn$nn.dist))
    ),
    directed = FALSE,
    vertices = data.frame(name = seq_len(n))
  )
  g <- igraph::simplify(g, edge.attr.comb = list(weight = "min"))

  el <- igraph::as_edgelist(g, names = FALSE)
  w  <- igraph::E(g)$weight

  # Candidates: edges that are long relative to the local scale at *both*
  # endpoints, i.e. that leave both neighbourhoods rather than staying inside.
  ratio <- w / pmin(local_scale[el[, 1]], local_scale[el[, 2]])
  cand  <- order(ratio, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(min(n_candidates, length(w)))]

  # Detour test. Deleting a local edge barely changes the graph distance
  # between its endpoints; deleting a short circuit forces the walk the whole
  # way around the fold. An edge whose deletion disconnects its endpoints
  # counts as a short circuit: there is no alternative route at all.
  is_short <- vapply(cand, function(e) {
    h <- igraph::delete_edges(g, e)
    d <- igraph::distances(h, v = el[e, 1], to = el[e, 2])[1, 1]
    !is.finite(d) || d > detour * w[e]
  }, logical(1))

  list(
    k          = k,
    components = igraph::components(g)$no,
    n_short    = sum(is_short),
    index      = sum(is_short) / n,          # short circuits per point
    edges      = el[cand[is_short], , drop = FALSE]
  )
}
```

The index is a lower bound: only the `n_candidates` longest-relative-to-scale
edges are tested, so raising the cap can only find more. Report the cap with the
number.

The second signature is local intrinsic dimension. A folded two-manifold still
measures as two-dimensional inside a facet and as more than two in a
neighbourhood straddling a crease, because that neighbourhood contains points
from two sheets. Estimating it per patch turns "how folded is this" into a
number. The TwoNN estimator [@facco2017twonn] uses only the two nearest
neighbours and so is itself local; the maximum-likelihood estimator of Levina
and Bickel [@levina2004intrinsic] is the usual alternative.

```{r decision-lid}
twonn_id <- function(X, discard = 0.10) {
  nn <- FNN::get.knn(X, k = 2)
  mu <- nn$nn.dist[, 2] / nn$nn.dist[, 1]
  mu <- sort(mu[is.finite(mu) & mu > 1])
  n    <- length(mu)
  keep <- seq_len(floor((1 - discard) * n))     # trim the heavy right tail
  x <- log(mu)[keep]
  y <- (-log(1 - (seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n))[keep]
  unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(y ~ x + 0))[1])  # slope through the origin
}

# Patchwise: the same estimator applied inside each of a sample of
# neighbourhoods, so the *spread* of local dimension is visible, not just a
# single global number.
local_id <- function(X, k = 50, sample_size = 500, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1]) {
  set.seed(seed)
  centres <- sample(nrow(X), min(sample_size, nrow(X)))
  nn <- FNN::get.knnx(X, X[centres, , drop = FALSE], k = k)
  vapply(seq_along(centres),
         function(i) twonn_id(X[nn$nn.index[i, ], , drop = FALSE]),
         numeric(1))
}
```

Now the validation. Sweep $\theta$ on the benchmark, compute the truth-free
index at each angle across `BENCH_SEEDS`, and mark the truth-based `theta_c`.
Sample size and $k$ are held at the values the real graph will have — both
statistics move with sampling density, and comparing a 2,638-cell graph against
a 300-point benchmark graph compares two different things.

```{r decision-calibrate, fig.alt="Fold angle on the horizontal axis from zero to just under pi over two, short circuits per point on the vertical axis. A solid median curve with a shaded ten-to-ninety percent seed ribbon sits flat at zero for small angles, then turns sharply upward and climbs steeply. A dashed vertical rule marks the fold angle returned by the truth-based short-circuit function; the rule falls at the same place the truth-free curve leaves zero."}
library(ggplot2)

thetas <- seq(0, pi / 2 - 0.05, length.out = 25)

calib <- do.call(rbind, lapply(thetas, function(th) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(BENCH_SEEDS, function(s) {
    m <- sample_manifold(pat, theta = th, n = N_CELLS, seed = s)
    data.frame(theta = th, seed = s,
               short_circuits = short_circuit_index(m$X, k = K_GRAPH)$index,
               lid = stats::median(local_id(m$X, k = 50, seed = s)))
  }))
}))

ggplot(calib, aes(theta, short_circuits)) +
  stat_summary(fun.min = function(z) stats::quantile(z, 0.1),
               fun.max = function(z) stats::quantile(z, 0.9),
               geom = "ribbon", alpha = 0.2) +
  stat_summary(fun = stats::median, geom = "line", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = theta_c, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = expression("fold angle " * theta),
       y = "short circuits per point")
```

Read the calibration backwards to place a dataset: compute the index on the real
$k$NN input, find where the benchmark's median curve crosses that value, and
take the corresponding $\theta$ as $\hat\theta$. The inversion is only as good
as the curve's slope — in the flat regime the curve is at zero for a range of
angles, so a zero index places the dataset in an interval, not at a point. Say
which.

## Reading the grid at the matched difficulty

With $\hat\theta$ in hand, the Chapter \@ref(results) grid becomes a lookup
rather than a league table. The relevant object is the slice at the matched fold
angle, not the column means over all $\theta$: methods swap rank across the
axis, which is the reason the axis exists, and a global winner is an average
over regimes you are not in.

```{r decision-grid-lookup}
# Wide grid written by scripts/run-benchmark-grid.R: one row per
# pattern x theta x noise x seed x method, with reconstruction error in `rmse`.
grid <- readRDS("data/processed/benchmark-grid.rds")

theta_hat <- 0.9   # read off the calibration above

slice <- subset(grid, pattern == "miura" & abs(theta - theta_hat) <= 0.05)

choice <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(slice, slice$method), function(d) {
  data.frame(method = d$method[1],
             med = stats::median(d$rmse),
             lo  = unname(stats::quantile(d$rmse, 0.1)),
             hi  = unname(stats::quantile(d$rmse, 0.9)))
}))
choice <- choice[order(choice$med), ]

# The decision rule. A method is *selected* only when its seed band is
# separated from the runner-up's. Otherwise the benchmark does not decide.
decided <- choice$hi[1] < choice$lo[2]
```

That last line is the part that matters. Chapter \@ref(results) reported how
much between-method variation falls inside within-method seed variance; over
much of the $\theta$ axis, a good deal of it does. The grid answers "which
method" only where the bands separate. Where they overlap, the honest output is
*the benchmark does not decide*, and the correct response is to report both
embeddings rather than to take the lower median and stop.

```{r decision-band, fig.alt="Horizontal box plots of Procrustes-aligned reconstruction error, one row per embedding method, ordered by median error, with individual seed results overplotted as points whose shape encodes the noise setting. The top two rows have visibly overlapping boxes; the remaining methods sit at clearly higher error with no overlap."}
ggplot(slice, aes(x = rmse, y = stats::reorder(method, rmse, stats::median))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.55) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = noise), alpha = 0.5,
             position = position_jitter(height = 0.15, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1])) +
  labs(x = expression("reconstruction error at " * hat(theta)),
       y = NULL, shape = "noise")
```

## A worked single-cell example

What follows is illustrative. One dataset, one preprocessing pipeline, one
downstream question. It is here to show the procedure end to end, not to
establish a fact about peripheral blood.

The data are the 10x Genomics PBMC set of Zheng and colleagues
[@zheng2017massively], in its widely redistributed 2,700-cell form. Accession,
version, file checksums and licence are recorded in Appendix \@ref(datasets).
The preprocessing is stated here in full because every diagnostic below is a
statement about the graph that preprocessing produces, and a different pipeline
produces a different graph [@luecken2019bestpractices].

```{r decision-pbmc-prep}
# Cells: >= 200 detected genes, < 5% mitochondrial counts.
# Genes: detected in >= 3 cells.
# Normalisation: counts per 10,000, then log1p.
# Feature selection: 2,000 highly variable genes, variance-stabilising ranking.
# Scaling: per gene, centred, unit variance.
# Reduction: 50 principal components.
# Graph: k = 20 nearest neighbours, Euclidean, on the 50 PCs.
counts <- Seurat::Read10X("data/raw/pbmc3k/filtered_gene_bc_matrices/hg19/")

obj <- Seurat::CreateSeuratObject(counts, min.cells = 3, min.features = 200)
obj[["percent_mt"]] <- Seurat::PercentageFeatureSet(obj, pattern = "^MT-")
obj <- subset(obj, subset = percent_mt < 5)
obj <- Seurat::NormalizeData(obj, scale.factor = 1e4)
obj <- Seurat::FindVariableFeatures(obj, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 2000)
obj <- Seurat::ScaleData(obj, features = Seurat::VariableFeatures(obj))
obj <- Seurat::RunPCA(obj, npcs = 50, verbose = FALSE)

pca_scores <- Seurat::Embeddings(obj, "pca")   # the matrix every metric sees
stopifnot(nrow(pca_scores) == N_CELLS)

# Populations, used only to label the panels below. Clustering is done on the
# same 50 PCs, never on the embedding.
obj <- Seurat::FindNeighbors(obj, dims = 1:50, k.param = K_GRAPH)
obj <- Seurat::FindClusters(obj, resolution = 0.5, verbose = FALSE)
cell_labels <- Seurat::Idents(obj)

obs_index <- short_circuit_index(pca_scores, k = K_GRAPH)$index
obs_lid   <- local_id(pca_scores, k = 50)
```

Two things follow immediately, and both are diagnostic rather than biological.
The local intrinsic dimension of the PBMC principal-component graph is neither
two nor close to it: patchwise TwoNN sits well above the intrinsic dimension of
any crease pattern in the benchmark, and it varies strongly between patches. The
short-circuit index is non-zero, and the suspect edges returned in `$edges` are
concentrated between the monocyte and dendritic-cell regions — exactly where two
populations approach one another in PCA space without being continuous.

Placing this dataset on the $\theta$ axis therefore requires an admission. The
short-circuit signature inverts to $\hat\theta \approx 0.9$ radians, of a
possible $\pi/2$. The intrinsic-dimension signature inverts to nothing: no fold
angle of a two-dimensional crease pattern produces local dimensions that high,
because the benchmark's intrinsic dimension is two by construction. The
benchmark's difficulty axis is one-dimensional. Real difficulty is not. Only the
first placement is used below, and only the claims that depend on the
short-circuit signature can lean on it.

Taking it that far: at $\hat\theta \approx 0.9$ the grid slice favours a
neighbour embedding over graph-geodesic methods, with $k$ at the upper end of
the tested range, because that is the regime in which short circuits have begun
to corrupt geodesic estimates while neighbour embeddings still recover local
structure. Applied to PBMC, that reads as UMAP at $k = 30$ rather than the field
default of $k = 15$ [@becht2019umap], with PCA initialisation rather than
spectral [@kobak2021initialization].

```{r decision-pbmc-embed, fig.alt="Two scatter plots side by side of the same 2,638 cells, the left panel produced with the field-default settings and the right with the benchmark-guided settings. Both show the same separated cell populations in different arrangements; populations are distinguished by marker shape as well as colour, and both panels are drawn with equal axis scaling."}
set.seed(BENCH_SEEDS[1])

default_cfg <- umap::umap.defaults
default_cfg$n_neighbors <- 15
default_cfg$init        <- "spectral"

guided_cfg <- default_cfg
guided_cfg$n_neighbors <- 30
guided_cfg$init        <- pca_scores[, 1:2]

emb <- rbind(
  data.frame(config = "field default",
             umap::umap(pca_scores, config = default_cfg)$layout),
  data.frame(config = "benchmark-guided",
             umap::umap(pca_scores, config = guided_cfg)$layout)
)
names(emb)[2:3] <- c("x", "y")
emb$label <- factor(rep(cell_labels, 2))

ggplot(emb, aes(x, y, colour = label, shape = label)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ config) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_book() +
  scale_shape_manual(values = seq_along(levels(emb$label))) +
  labs(x = "UMAP 1", y = "UMAP 2", colour = NULL, shape = NULL)
```

### The null result

The benchmark-guided configuration did not beat the field default in any way
that survives inspection. The same populations separate. Cluster assignments
agree to within the disagreement produced by re-seeding either configuration.
The larger $k$ moves the panels visibly, but the aggregate neighbourhood
statistics move by less than the seed-to-seed spread of either configuration on
its own — which is precisely the condition under which Chapter \@ref(results)
says the grid does not decide, and the correct reading is that it did not decide
here either.

This is worth stating plainly, because the alternative is worse. The procedure
was run, the outcome was a null, and reporting the null is the only version of
this chapter consistent with the rest of the book. What the benchmark changed
was not the picture but the reporting: it named specific suspect edges and where
they are, it supplied a seed band against which to compare the two
configurations, and it removed the temptation to read the shape of either panel
as structure. Those are real deliverables. A different embedding was not one of
them.

## The decision procedure

What the benchmark licenses, in the order you would run it. Each item
corresponds to a result in Part III rather than to a preference.

1. **State the graph, not the data.** Every method and every metric downstream
   sees the neighbourhood graph on your reduced representation. Record the
   normalisation, feature selection, number of components, distance and $k$.
   Two pipelines differing in any of these are being compared on different
   objects.
2. **Run the short-circuit diagnostic before choosing a method.** If the index
   is non-zero, graph-geodesic methods are compromised by construction and no
   hyperparameter search repairs it. Report the index, the candidate cap and
   the $k$ it was computed at.
3. **Estimate local intrinsic dimension and look at its spread.** A wide spread
   across patches means no single $k$ is right everywhere, and a single-$k$
   embedding is a compromise you should state.
4. **Place the dataset on the $\theta$ axis at matched $n$ and $k$.** Where the
   diagnostics disagree about the placement, as they did above, say so and use
   the more pessimistic one.
5. **Read the grid at the matched slice, not the global ranking.** Method order
   changes across $\theta$; that is the finding, not an artefact.
6. **Apply the separation rule.** Select a method only when its seed band is
   disjoint from the runner-up's. Otherwise report both embeddings and say the
   benchmark did not decide.
7. **Re-run across at least 20 seeds and show the spread.** A single embedding
   is one draw from a distribution whose width you have not measured.
8. **Never report trustworthiness, continuity or $k$NN preservation alone.**
   Chapter \@ref(evaluation) showed they are high on embeddings that are wrong.
   Report them with the $k$ they were computed at and with the caveat that they
   score the objective the embedding optimised.
9. **Verify every claim made from the embedding in the original space.** If two
   populations look adjacent, test adjacency on the high-dimensional
   representation. The embedding is a figure, not evidence.
10. **Report the null.** If the benchmark-guided choice does not beat the
    default, that is a result about the benchmark's reach and belongs in the
    paper.

## Back to Chari and Pachter

Chari and Pachter argue that two-dimensional embeddings of high-dimensional
single-cell data are so distorted as to be misleading, and that the field's
reliance on them is a methodological error [@chari2023specious]. The benchmark
lets us separate what we can support by measurement from what we cannot.

Supported. Distortion is real, large, and measurable rather than arguable: at
moderate and high $\theta$ the reconstruction error against exact truth is
substantial for every method tested, and the embeddings that look most
convincing are not the most accurate. The standard neighbourhood metrics do not
detect this — they scored highly on embeddings with large true error, which is
the strongest form of the claim that current evaluation practice cannot
distinguish good embeddings from bad ones. And seed variance is wide enough that
single-run figures, which is what the literature almost always publishes, are
anecdotes.

Not supported. The critique is sometimes read as implying that two-dimensional
embeddings are useless in general. The benchmark contradicts that: below the
short-circuit angle several methods recover the true unfolding to within noise,
and the failure is regime-dependent rather than universal. The useful question
is not "is the embedding distorted" but "how distorted, and can I tell from the
data" — and the diagnostics above answer the second half. Second, the critique's
own quantitative apparatus is built from neighbourhood-preservation measures,
and Chapter \@ref(evaluation) showed those measures to be unreliable in exactly
the regime where the argument needs them. The conclusion may well be right; the
instrument used to reach it inherits the weakness it is being used to expose.
Third, the benchmark says nothing about whether the biological conclusions drawn
from published embeddings are wrong. It cannot. It measures geometry.

Kobak and Berens argue the other side — that careful use of t-SNE, with
attention to initialisation and perplexity, recovers structure well
[@kobak2019art]. The benchmark is compatible with both positions, which is the
uncomfortable but honest reading: method quality is a curve over difficulty, and
two authors evaluating at different points on that curve will disagree
permanently without either being wrong.

## Honest limits

This is a benchmark on synthetic, isometric, uniformly sampled manifolds of
intrinsic dimension two, or $2k$ under the product construction of Chapter
\@ref(benchmarks). Every one of those adjectives is a limit.

*Isometric* is the strongest. The whole ground-truth claim rests on rigid
folding preserving distances along the surface, which is what makes the flat
pattern the exact answer and what lets `dist(truth)` stand in for geodesic
distance without approximation. Real data have no flat chart. A manifold with
intrinsic curvature cannot be unfolded to the plane without distortion, so for
real data there is generally no correct two-dimensional embedding to recover —
only better and worse compromises. The benchmark measures how methods behave
when a correct answer exists. It cannot measure how they behave when one does
not.

*Uniformly sampled* excludes the density variation that dominates real
neighbourhood graphs. *Intrinsic dimension two* is far below any plausible
estimate for a transcriptome, as the PBMC diagnostic showed directly.
*Synthetic* excludes the measurement model entirely: counting noise, dropout,
doublets, ambient RNA and batch structure are absent, and each deforms the graph
in ways this benchmark cannot reproduce. And the clusters that dominate
single-cell embeddings are not manifold structure at all — a crease pattern is
connected, and much of what a UMAP of PBMC shows is not.

The strongest claims the benchmark licenses are therefore about metrics and
failure modes, not about biology. It establishes that trustworthiness and its
relatives can certify wrong embeddings, that short circuits are detectable
without ground truth, and that seed variance is routinely larger than method
differences. Those claims transfer because they are claims about algorithms.
Anything of the form "therefore your cell types are wrong" does not follow, and
is not being argued here.

## Reporting standards

The standing rules of this book exist because of results in Part III, and they
are what should survive contact with a manuscript.

Every figure carries alt text describing the structure shown, not the caption
repeated. No result is encoded by colour alone: population identity gets shape
or facet as well, mountain and valley creases get linetype as well as colour,
and a figure that fails in greyscale fails. Seeds are disclosed — which seeds,
how many, and the spread across them — and stochastic embeddings are shown as
several draws or as a summary over draws, never as one run presented as the
result.

Aspect ratio is the standard that gets skipped. An embedding is defined up to a
similarity transform at best — that is exactly what `reconstruction_error()`
quotients out — so the two axes carry the same units and must be drawn at the
same scale. `coord_equal()` is not decoration. Stretching one axis to fill a
panel changes apparent cluster shape, apparent separation and apparent density,
which are precisely the quantities readers extract from these figures. Axis
units on a UMAP or t-SNE panel are not interpretable in any case, and the honest
treatment is to draw them to equal scale and label them as coordinates rather
than as measurements.

None of this makes an embedding correct. It makes the figure an accurate report
of what the algorithm produced, which is the most a two-dimensional picture of
high-dimensional data can honestly claim to be.
